title: Protocol for extracting live blastoderm cells from embryos of annual killifish
protocol: Add 1.5 g of base and 0.1 g of crosslinker in a petri dish of 35 mm diameter.
Mix PDMS carefully for at least 3 min by stirring with a plastic disposable pipette, ensuring all mixture including corners is stirred.
Place the mixed PDMS in a vacuum chamber and apply negative pressure below 500 mmHg for at least 5 min to degas the mixture.
Add 15 g of base and 1 g of crosslinker directly into a petri dish of 100 mm diameter.
Mix PDMS carefully for at least 5 min by stirring with a plastic disposable pipette, ensuring all mixture including corners is stirred.
Place the mixed PDMS in a vacuum chamber and apply negative pressure below 500 mmHg for at least 5 min to degas the mixture.
If vacuum chamber and negative pressure pump are not present, leave PDMS mixtures for 30 min to allow gas bubbles to come to the surface.
Break bubbles by strong mechanical action, such as firm knocking of the petri dish bottom against a table.
Transfer the PDMS dishes in the oven and cure the PDMS mixture for 1 h at 80°C on a plane surface.
If an oven is not present, cure PDMS mixtures overnight at room temperature.
Cut the thick layer of PDMS to form the wells for the bursting chambers.
Remove the thick layer of PDMS from the petri dish using a round-tip tweezer and place it on the lid of the same petri dish.
Detach the PDMS from the dish by passing the tip of the tweezer along the border and then pulling it out.
Cut its edges of the slab of PDMS using a bistoury.
Punch 4 through holes of 8 mm diameter using an appropriate biopsy punch to form the wells of the bursting chamber.
Work in clean conditions and avoid getting dust and dirt on the PDMS to ensure good bonding.
Use clean tweezers to manipulate the PDMS, avoiding bare hands or gloves that may leave a layer of skin oil or powder.
Mount the PDMS slab with wells onto the thin PDMS layer in the dish.
Gently press the slab against the surface of the dish using tweezers to ensure adhesion and squeeze out air bubbles between the two layers.
Leave the device in the oven at 80°C for 3 hours to improve bonding.
Fill the chambers with 50 μL each of Pluronic acid solution.
Incubate for 2 hours at room temperature.
Wash chambers 4 times using dH2O by adding 50 μL of Milli-Q H2O and removing it using a p200 pipette.
Let them dry and sterilize under UV light for 15 minutes before use.
Maintain ambient temperature at 25°C ± 2°C for enzymatic hair removal from N. furzeri eggs.
Use a plastic Pasteur pipette to gently place individual N. furzeri eggs into glass tubes, with a maximum of 5 eggs per tube.
Use glass tubes for handling eggs after pronase treatment to prevent adherence and breakage.
Add at least 200 μL of modified Yamamoto solution (S3) and incubate for 10 minutes.
Remove the modified Yamamoto solution (S3) and repeat this washing step three times.
After washing, remove salt-tris buffer (S4) and add 200 μL of pronase solution (S5), then incubate at 25°C for 40 minutes.
If hair digestion is incomplete after 40 minutes, continue the incubation for another 30 minutes as needed.
Inspect eggs frequently using a stereoscope to confirm complete removal of hair.
Remove pronase solution (S5) and wash eggs three times with DMEM/F-12 media containing EGTA.
Observe eggs under a stereoscope; they should appear clean with a smooth surface. If not, discard the eggs as prolonged treatment can damage them.
Remove soil from the embryo surface mechanically.
Use a plastic Pasteur pipette to gently place one egg on a dry clean wipe.
Use a paintbrush dipped in DMEM/F-12 media to carefully move and rotate the egg.
Brush and rotate the egg for at least 2 minutes with at least 1 mL of media.
Collect the cleaned egg using a plastic Pasteur pipette.
Place the collected egg in a 15 mL falcon tube containing 1 mL DMEM/F-12 media.
Repeat the cleaning process for all eggs.
Discard any egg that deflates or breaks during the cleaning process.
Remove the DMEM/F-12 media from the cleaned eggs and add 5 mL of chlorine solution.
Incubate the eggs in the chlorine solution for 5 minutes to disinfect them.
Wash the eggs three times using DMEM/F-12 media with EGTA.
Discard any eggs that do not appear smooth under a stereoscope.
Place one egg in the bursting chamber.
Add 50 μL of DMEM/F-12 media with EGTA to the bursting chamber.
Position the bursting chamber under a stereoscope for high precision manipulation of the egg.
Puncture the egg using a pair of fine-pointed tweezers.
Gently puncture the egg using the tip to partly release the high pressure.
Peel off the chorion carefully from the opposite side of the puncture until all chorion detaches from the egg.
Fill the bursting chamber to the brim, avoiding overfilling which can cause a convex meniscus.
Gently but firmly hold the egg using a tweezer in the non-dominant hand.
Use the tip of another tweezer to gently puncture the chorion to release internal pressure.
Avoid applying too much pressure when puncturing to prevent embryo bursting and cell death.
Care must be taken not to accidentally remove the egg from the chamber during puncturing.
A small amount of egg content will be released after puncturing.
Flow of fluid may move the EVL toward the puncture, obstructing the hole.
Peel the chorion carefully using precise tweezers.
Gently grab the chorion with both tweezers on the opposite side of the puncture.
Pull the chorion apart to create a small opening (approximately ¼ of the diameter of the embryo).
Grab opposite sides of the small opening made in step 20a and pull the whole chorion apart to release the embryo.
Remove the content of the bursting chamber using a p200 micropipette.
Place the removed content in a sterile Eppendorf 1.5 mL tube.
Cut approximately 5 mm of the tip of the p200 micropipette before use.
Wash twice the well with additional 50 μL DMEM/F-12 media with EGTA.
Place all the media collected in the same Eppendorf tube.
Repeat the protocol for all the embryos and pool the extracts together to a maximum of five dechorionated embryos per Eppendorf tube.
Gently mix the DMEM/F-12 media with EGTA containing the dechorionated embryos using a p200 pipette set to 50 μL to separate lipid droplets in the yolk from the rest of the embryo.
Use DMEM/F-12 media with EGTA for dissociation.
Apply sufficient shear stress using pipetting with an intact p200 pipette tip, approximately 10 times.
Spin the Eppendorf tubes in a cell culture centrifuge at 200 × g for 5 minutes.
Discard the supernatant carefully to avoid disturbing the pellet.
Remove the supernatant from the air-liquid interface to remove lipids and other light components of the yolk.
Add 300 μL of DMEM/F-12 media to the solution.
Gently resuspend the solution using a p200 pipette.
Centrifuge the solution again.
Resuspend the pellet in 300 μL of DMEM/F-12 media using a p200 pipette.
Repeat centrifugation and resuspension steps with DMEM/F-12 media to remove undesired embryonic residues.
After the last centrifugation, resuspend the pellet in 100 μL of DMEM/F-12 media using a P200 pipette.
Count viable cells by Calcein-AM assay at 25°C ± 2°C.
Measure cell viability and yield using standard cell counting methods (Neubauer chamber).
Centrifuge the cell suspension obtained in step 28 of previous session at 200 × g for 5 min and discard the supernatant using a p200 pipette.
Resuspend the cell pellet in 10 μL DMEM/F-12 media containing Calcein AM.
Incubate for 20 min at 25°C.
Pipette 10 μl of cell solution into a Neubauer chamber with a glass cover on top.
Using a fluorescence microscope, count the number of cells with green fluorescence in each quadrant.
Calculate the average cell number per quadrant.
Count the number of non-fluorescence cells to obtain the ratio between viable and non-viable cells.
Calculate the average number of counted cells per volume of each quadrant (0.1 μL).
Multiply the number of cells per microliter by the total volume (10 μL) to determine the total number of cells.
Divide the total number of cells by the number of embryos (5) to find the number of cells per embryo.
Use a fraction of the cell suspension obtained in step 28 for routine checks on cell viability and yield.
